title: Manifest Emotions Explained Further
paragraphs: Meyppāṭu is an inner feeling manifesting on one’s body for others to see and hear. Watery eyes, beads of tears, bristling of hair, perspiration, shivering and other such overt signs are the meyppāṭus arising out of the mind’s response to an external event.

Suppose a person faces a python coming to swallow him, it is natural for him to be subjected to shivering of the body, anxiety to escape and perspiration. The python here is the external event (cuvaippaṭuporuḷ) that causes the manifestation of the emotions (cuvai) on the person, whose tripidation and bewilderment are the signs (kuṟippu) and perspiration and shivering are the physical expressions (viṟal). These things together, as they come to be known to others are described by the term meyppāṭu.

It has been the part of literary conventions from the ancient times to represent these sentiments arising out of our inner life and external life situations and experiences in dramatic usage and imaginative usage.
The Tolkāppiyam verse in this regard occurs as the first verse of the Meyppāṭṭiyal section:
> As the literate men say, > Thirty-two are the sources > That represent spheres of human sport > Wherein are born the eight emotions > With each emotion having four sources.
There are thirty-two sources of human sport wherein are born things sixteen when classified.

Music and dance enjoyed in those days by the three crowned monarchs and the chieftains, the emotions that they experienced as they witnessed these ‘sports’ (paṇṇai), the objects of these emotions (cuvaippaṭuporuḷ), the inner responses they felt (kuṟippu) and their external manifestations (viṟal) - these four expand into thirty-two as is seen in the Tolkāppiyam verse above.
